findings.claim: Section A of your listening exam plays short unfamiliar extracts from across this period and asks you to name the era, the instruments and the way the sound is built.
findings.truth: Section A has unfamiliar-listening questions covering all four areas of study, not only Western classical tradition 1650–1910.

findings.claim: Valved brass instruments, invented in the 1810s–30s, let horns and trumpets play a full scale instead of only the notes of a bugle call.
findings.truth: Valves made chromatic playing easier, but natural horns could already produce a chromatic scale by hand-stopping. The first successful valved horn dates to 1814; the bass tuba appeared in 1835.
findings.evidence: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Cor d'orchestre and Horn in F; Yamaha, The Birth of the Tuba

findings.claim: That sentence names the instrument, the technique and the moment — three marking points in one line.
findings.truth: The specification gives no fixed three-point allocation for a sentence of this kind.

findings.claim: A bare label without evidence rarely scores full marks.
findings.truth: The specification does not set a general full-mark rule for identifying structure; individual questions may require only an identification.

findings.claim: Section B marks come from three things: naming the musical element, giving its correct technical term, and saying where in the music it happens.
findings.truth: Section B assesses written analysis and evaluation using musical elements and contexts; it cannot be reduced to a fixed three-part marking formula.

findings.claim: This names the passage, uses correct terms, and locates it precisely — the kind of sentence that scores full marks.
findings.truth: Section B contains short and extended linked questions, so a single sentence cannot generally be said to score full marks.

findings.claim: The six practice answers allocate stated marks to individual points, for example '1 mark for' and 'Up to 4 marks'.
findings.truth: AQA specifies the assessment and section totals, not these bespoke question totals or point-by-point allocations. If the activity is revised, use numberless answer guidance across the full practice set.

findings.claim: That freedom to shape dynamics for dramatic effect, rather than because an instrument could not do otherwise, is where the Romantic era begins.
findings.truth: Either retain this as a metaphorical transition or recast it as Beethoven foreshadowing later Romantic tendencies. No single use of dynamics establishes the start of the Romantic era, and period boundaries are interpretive.
findings.evidence: Eastman School of Music, Beethoven Symphony Basics; Beethovenfest, Beethoven: Symphony No. 1

summary: Six verified surgical edits correct assessment advice and brass-instrument history. Three low-severity notes flag unsupported bespoke practice marking; one interpretive period-boundary claim is left for adjudication.
